faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Orangeburg attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.

faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Orangeburg attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Holly Hill home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes our crew is called about here are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and — only in the wet coastal and swamp country — the cottonmouth. We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is never handled as a removal job, and venomous snakes are safety-and-referral work, not a guaranteed capture.

Elloree.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Elloree and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the Lake Marion-side farm town in the county's northeast. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in pine-straw beds and lawns, then about opossums in crawlspaces.

Older homes near the town center give way to ranch subdivisions and then to farmhouses on the outskirts, and the wildlife entries change with each ring. Pine straw is the Midlands detail that matters most: copperheads vanish into it, armadillos root through it, and raccoons cross it nightly from creek woods to rooftops.

Before we leave a Elloree home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: I found a bat inside my Santee home. What should I do?
faqs.a: No permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina, but the calendar matters. We follow SCDNR guidance: full exclusions in March–April or August–October, and no complete exclusion during the May to mid-July pup season, when young bats cannot fly out. The work itself is one-way exits plus sealing every secondary gap around the rooflines near Lake Marion shore and I-95 corridor at the county's east end. If a bat turns up inside the living space of your Santee home, keep people and pets away from it — bats found indoors should be submitted for rabies testing through the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my Santee house?
faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a Santee job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near Lake Marion shore and I-95 corridor at the county's east end with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.

Santee.wildlife_intro:
The pattern in Santee is set by the Lake Marion shore and I-95 corridor at the county's east end. If we had to name this town's signature jobs, they would be gray squirrels in mature pine canopy and raccoons working creek corridors.

Brick ranches from the 1960s and 1970s, older in-town homes near the center, and fast-growing subdivisions at the edges give this housing stock three distinct generations of rooflines to inspect. River and lake country surrounds these neighborhoods — creeks, coves, and wooded drains run behind the subdivisions — giving raccoons, squirrels, and bats a covered route to almost every roofline.

Every job in Santee ends the same way it should: openings found on the inspection closed in steel mesh and flashing, so the house near Lake Marion shore and I-95 corridor at the county's east end stops advertising vacancies to the next animal that passes.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Bowman home?

What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.
